*reasoning in my own voice:*

Aiyo, 70 years old already, and still I'm out in these cotton fields. My old man and me, just the two of us in the house now. The children all went out to work years ago, but my daughter comes back in autumn when the cotton opens — she knows I can't pick 8 mu alone anymore, my back can't take it.

Cotton is what I know. I've planted cotton on this land for — I can't even count. Before the double-cropping came to the eastern villages, everybody here planted cotton, and I never changed. My hands know cotton. I don't need to read anything to plant cotton.

This year, like every year, I do what I've always done. After Qingming passes and the ground warms up proper — around the middle of the fourth month — I'll plant. I buy the seed at the town market, the same kind my neighbor Old Wang buys. He picks good varieties, I trust him. No point saving my own seed for cotton, the seed people sell these days is better, they say it doesn't get the worms so bad.

Before planting, my nephew brings his little tractor and plows the 8 mu for me. I pay him something, but he's family so not full price. We lay the plastic film — without the film the cotton doesn't come up well, everybody uses film now. I put one bag of compound fertilizer on each mu before planting, the same kind I always buy, the one with the numbers on it. Then when the cotton is flowering, around the sixth month, I scatter some urea around the plants, maybe half a bag per mu, not too much — urea is expensive and if I put too much the plants grow tall leaves but few bolls, my grandmother told me that when I was young.

Watering — I have the well, so I water twice usually. Once when the seedlings need to come up strong if the spring is dry, and once when the bolls are forming, because that's when cotton really needs water. Three times if it's a very dry year. The electricity for the pump costs money, so I don't water more than I need.

For the bugs, the seed these days is the kind that kills the bollworm by itself, so I don't spray so much for worms. But the aphids still come, and the weeds, so I spray maybe two, three times in the season. I buy the cheap medicine at the store, whatever Old Wang's wife tells me works that year.

How much will I pick? In a good year maybe 500 jin per mu of seed cotton, in a bad year 400. Last year was okay, not great — some of the bolls didn't open well because of the cool weather in autumn. This year, I hope for a normal year. I can't handle much more, and I can't handle much less either — if the price is bad we just eat less meat.

Money-wise, I try not to spend more than I have. No credit, I don't borrow. If the fertilizer gets too expensive one year, I use a little less. That's how we've always gotten through.
